newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai tapioca exports pressured by EU grain surplus.
newsitem.headline: Thai tapioca exports pressured by EU grain surplus.

text.p: Thai tapioca exports face a tough time next year on an expected grain surplus and falling feed material prices in the European Union, government and industry sources said on Thursday.
They said although Thai tapioca exports are expected to at least maintain their 1996 level, they will likely earn less foreign exchange.
According to a preliminary forecast by the commerce ministry, Thailand will ship out 3.5-4.0 million tonnes of tapioca this year, 90 percent of which will go to to the EU.
"The demand is still there but we have to compete with wheat, barley and other grains," said Seree Denworalak, head of the Thai Tapioca Trade Association.
A senior commerce ministry official told Reuters that Thailand was weighing measures to maintain its competitiveness as a major exporter.

The official said the measures included plans to develop new markets, especially Russia and North Korea, and to encourage farmers to trim production costs by switching to new high-yield strains of tapioca.
"Our tapioca prices will have to be low to be competitive," the official said.
Thailand hopes the new strains will raise the yield of cassava roots to 30-49 tonnes per hectare from a current average of 16 tonnes.
The commerce ministry estimated that the EU will produce bumper crops of about 204 million tonnes of grain in the 1996/97 crop year up from 175 million tonnes the previous year.
Thai tapioca pellets were quoted at $105-110 FOB Bangkok this week against $120-130 early this year.

He said tapioca prices could ease further, making the product more attractive as feed material in the EU. He said expected lower prices of soymeal, used for mixing with tapioca, would also boost demand for the Thai commodity.
He cautioned, however, that if rising non-feed usage of tapioca roots in Thailand raised local prices of the commodity, its competitiveness in EU would be eroded.

The Thai government mostly bases its allocation of annual EU quotas on stocks held by exporters who are encouraged to help maintain domestic prices by buying fresh tapioca harvests during the height of the production season.
Seree of the Tapioca Association said developing new markets was not easy and potential new markets such as Russia and North Korea pose high credit risks for Thai exporters.
